translations.text: March 12. The martyrdom of Saint Pionius, priest of the city of Smyrna.
The apostle commands us to share in the commemoration of the saints, knowing
that whoever commemorates them wholeheartedly and with faith also spurs others on,
as they seek to imitate greater things. And it is especially fitting to remember Pionius the martyr,
because, while he was in the world, he turned many away from error, having been an apostolic man among us.
And at the end, when he was called to the Lord and suffered martyrdom, he left this written account for our instruction,
so that even to this day we might preserve the memory of his teaching. On the second day of the sixth month,
as the Great Sabbath approached, in the days when the blessed martyr Polycarp was born,
during the persecution under Emperor Decius in Smyrna, Pionius the priest was arrested,
together with Sabina the confessor, Asclepiades, Macedonius,
and Limnus, a priest of the catholic Church. Pionius had foreseen it one day beforehand,
on the day when Polycarp was born—was born—that in those days these people would be arrested, together with Sabina
and Asclepiades, while they were fasting. And when he saw that they would be arrested the next morning,
he took three twisted cords and placed them around his own neck and those of Sabina and Asclepiades.
And they waited, sitting in the house. He did this for the sake of those who knew them,
so that no one would suppose that they, like others, were going to defile themselves with sacrifices, but so that everyone would see
that they intended to go straight to prison. After they had prayed and eaten bread and drunk water,
on the Great Sabbath, Polemon came to them with those who accompanied him,
to seek out Christians and drag them away to sacrifices and defilement. And Polemon said,
“I know, Pionius, the emperor’s commands: he orders you to sacrifice to the gods.”
Pionius said, “I know God’s commands, in which he orders us to worship him alone.”
Polemon said, “Then come to the assembly, so that you may declare this there.” And Asclepiades and Sabina said,
“We obey the living God and declare our allegiance to him.” Then Polemon led them away.
And when they arrived, everyone saw that they were wearing bonds.
And the crowds hurried as fast as they could, as though to see a most glorious wonder, so that they pushed one another aside.
When they arrived at the place where the people had gathered, that whole place was filled.
The stairways and upper rooms too were filled with Greeks and Jews, and [?] were celebrating, since it was the great Sabbath.
They placed them in their midst, and Polemon said, “Pionius, submit, as everyone else does,
and offer sacrifice, so that you will not be tortured.” Pionius stretched out his hand and, with a radiant face, answered:
“Men who pride yourselves on the beauty of Smyrna, and you Jews who have come among them,
listen to me while I speak to you briefly. For I hear concerning those who come forward of their own accord
that you laugh and rejoice, treating as a game the transgression of those who sacrifice against their will.
You Greeks ought to obey your teacher Homer, who advises:
‘It is not right to boast over the dying.’ And as for you Jews, Moses commands:
‘If you see your enemy’s donkey fallen beneath its load, do not pass it by,
but be sure to help it up.’ Likewise Solomon says, ‘If your enemy falls, do not rejoice,
and do not exalt yourself when he stumbles.’ For I obey my own teacher. I choose rather to die
than to transgress his word, and I strive to change what I formerly learned
and afterward also taught. At whom, then, are the Jews laughing?
Even if we are their enemies, as they say, we are nevertheless human beings who hate injustice.
Let us say whom we have wronged, whom we have driven away, whom we have killed, or whom we have forced
to worship idols. Or do they think their own sins are equal to those of people who now act out of fear of men?
But they are better only insofar as voluntary sins are better than involuntary ones. Who, then, forced the Jews to sacrifice to Baal-peor,
or to eat sacrifices offered to the dead, or to commit sexual immorality with foreign women, or to burn their sons and daughters as offerings to idols,
or to grumble against God, or to oppose Moses, or to be ungrateful to their benefactors,
or to turn back to Egypt in their hearts, or, when Moses had gone up to receive the law,
to say to Aaron, ‘Make gods for us,’ and to make a calf? They can deceive you,
even though the books of Judges, Kings, and Exodus are read to you,
and all the other books in which they are exposed. Yet they ask why these people come forward of their own accord to sacrifice, without being forced.
Do you then reproach all Christians because of these people? Do you think that this present life is like a flowing stream?
Which heap is larger, the heap of chaff or the heap of wheat? For when the worker comes with a winnowing shovel to clear the threshing floor,
the chaff, being light, is easily carried away by the wind, but the wheat remains there.
Look again at a net that has been cast: is everything it gathers useful?
So too is this present life. How, then, do you wish, in this matter,
us to suffer—as righteous people or as unrighteous people? But even if as unrighteous people,
how is it, then, that you too, accused of those unrighteous deeds, do the same things?
But if as righteous people, when the righteous suffer, what hope can you have?
For if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly person and the sinner appear? For judgment is coming upon the world,
of which we have been assured by many. I myself went away and traveled through the whole land of Judea.
And after crossing the Jordan, I saw the land still bearing witness to this day
to the wrath of God that came upon it because of those who committed sins and lived there,
killing strangers and committing many other acts of violence. I saw smoke rising from it to this day,
and the land reduced to ashes by fire and devoid of all fruit and moisture.
I also saw the Dead Sea, its water changed, having departed from its natural state through fear of God,
and unable to sustain any living thing within itself. If anyone goes into it beneath the water, it casts him out,
and it cannot hold a human body within itself. For it does not wish to receive a human being, lest on account of a human being
it be rebuked again. And these things I tell you of are far away. You have seen and tell of the land of Lydia and Decapolis,
burned by fire and lying there to this day
as a warning to the ungodly. Etna on the island of Sicily, and the fire coming out of it.
Even if this too is far from you, consider the hot water coming out of the earth.
And consider where it is set ablaze or where it is heated, if there is no fire beneath the earth.
Therefore I proclaim to you that there will be a judgment by fire from God,
through his Word, Jesus Christ. And for this reason we do not serve your gods
or bow down to the golden idol. When Pionius had said these and many other things,
Polemon and those with him and the whole crowd fell silent and listened.
so that no one dared utter a sound. Pionius said again, “We do not serve your gods.”
“And we will not bow down to the golden idol.” They brought them into the midst and assigned some men from the council, together with Polemon, to attend to them.
They pleaded with him, saying, “Listen to us, Pionius, for we love you.
For many reasons you deserve to live. Because of your good character and gentleness, it is good for you to live,
and to see this light, and much else.” But he said to them, “I too say that
it is good to live. But what we love is better, and that light is the true light.
All this is indeed good, and we flee, hating the works of God. But we desire other, greater things,
and disregard these.” Alexander, [?], a deceitful man, said, “Listen to us, Pionius.”
Pionius said, “You listen to me. For what you know, I know,
but what I know, you do not know.” Alexander wanted to mock him
and said mockingly, “Why, then, are these chains on you?” Pionius said, “For this reason:
so that those passing through your city will not think that we have come after sacrificing and defiling ourselves.
And so that you may know that we do not even demand to be questioned, but go to prison willingly,
and not at the will of others. You seize us and lead us away, but since we are wearing chains, leave us alone.
For you will not lead us in chains to your idols.” At this Alexander fell silent.
Again, as they pleaded with him, he said to him,
“This is what we have resolved and set our hearts on.” And he rebuked them at length and told them about the things to come.
Alexander said, “What use, then, are these words of yours to us? Because of them, you are not even worthy to live.”
As the crowd wanted to hold a public gathering in the theater so that they could hear more, some men came from the governor and said to Polemon,
“Do not let him speak, lest they enter the theater and there be an uproar and an inquiry about him.”
Hearing this, Polemon said, “Pionius, if you do not want to sacrifice, at least come to the place of the idols.”
But he said, “Your idols will gain nothing if we go there.”
Polemon said, “Listen to us, Pionius.” Pionius said, “If only I could persuade you to become Christians!”
They laughed loudly and said, “You will not make us do that and be burned alive.” Pionius said, “It is far worse to burn after death.”
When Sabina smiled, Polemon and those with him said, “Are you laughing?” She said, “Yes, if God wills.”
“For I am a Christian. All who believe in Christ will laugh in everlasting joy.”
He said to her, “You will have to undergo what you do not want. For women who do not sacrifice are put into prostitution.”
She said, “It is for the holy Lord to take care of that.” Then Polemon spoke again to Pionius:
“Let us persuade you, Pionius.” Pionius said, “Have you been ordered to persuade or to torture?
If you cannot persuade, then torture.” Then Polemon questioned him and said, “Sacrifice, Pionius.” Pionius said,
“I am a Christian.” Polemon said, “What god do you worship?” Pionius said, “God Almighty,
who made heaven and earth and everything in them, and all of us, who gives us every abundance,
whom we have come to know through his Word, Jesus Christ.” Polemon said, “Then sacrifice according to the emperor’s command.”
Pionius said, “I do not offer sacrifices to a human being, for I am a Christian.”
Polemon said, “Are you a Christian?” Pionius said, “Yes.” Polemon said, “Of what church?”
He answered, “The catholic Church, for there is no other from Christ.” Then he turned to Sabina.
For Pionius had told her beforehand, “Call yourself Theodota, so that your name does not cause you to fall again
into the hands of your lawless former mistress.” For her mistress, in the time of Emperor Gordian,
wishing to turn Sabina away from the faith, had bound her and driven her away. Later, while she was with Pionius, she was arrested
during that persecution. So Polemon said to her too, “What is your name?” She said, “Theodota.”
He said, “Are you a Christian?” She said, “Yes, I am a Christian.”
Polemon said, “Of what church?” Sabina said, “The catholic Church.” Polemon said, “What god do you worship?”
Sabina said, “The Almighty, who made heaven and earth and all of us,
whom we have come to know through his Word, Jesus Christ.” Then Polemon questioned Asclepiades:
“Are you a Christian too?” Asclepiades said, “Yes.” Polemon said, “Of what church?”
Asclepiades said, “The catholic Church.” Polemon said, “What god do you worship?” Asclepiades
said, “Jesus Christ.” Polemon said, “Is this, then, a different god?”
Asclepiades said, “No, but the same one whom these two named.” When these things had been said, they led them to prison.
A large crowd followed, so that all the streets were full.
Some were saying about Pionius, “How is it that, though he is always pale, his face is now rosy?”
As Sabina held him by his clothes to keep from being pulled away by the crowd,
some said mockingly, “Auntie is afraid she will be pulled away!” Then one of them shouted,
“If they will not sacrifice, let them be tortured!” Someone else said, “Look, this man is going to sacrifice!”
He was referring to Asclepiades, who was with us. Pionius said, “You are lying!
Asclepiades is not doing that.” Others said, “This man and that man have offered sacrifice.”
Pionius said, “Everyone has his own free will. What is that to you? My name is Pionius.”
When he had said this, they brought them into prison with difficulty, hemmed in as they were by the crowd,
and handed them over to the guards. When they entered, they found a presbyter of the catholic church named Limnus imprisoned there,
along with a Macedonian woman and a man of the Phrygian faith named Eutychian.
While they were together, the prison guards learned that the things brought by the faithful
were not being accepted by Pionius’s companions. For Pionius said, “When our need was greater,
we were a burden to no one. How, then, should we accept anything now?” The prison guards became angry,
and in their anger they took them farther inside, so that they would receive no kindness at all.
But they glorified God and fell silent. He gave them what they usually received, so that the guards repented
and brought them out of the prison again to the front. But they stayed where they were, saying, “Glory to the Lord!
For this has turned out for our good. We have room both to talk and to pray to God, day and night.”
Nevertheless, many people from the surrounding region came even into the prison, wishing to persuade them.
When they heard their answer, they marveled. There also came in those who were being dragged away by force
from among the Christian brothers, weeping greatly all the time, especially over the good men
and those who had led good lives. This made Pionius weep and say, “Senselessly, senselessly you torment us!
Senselessly you cut us down, as you see the Church’s pearls trampled by pigs and the stars of heaven swept by the serpent’s tail
down to the earth, and the vineyard planted by God’s right hand ravaged by pigs.
Now everyone passing by plunders it. My children, whom I am again bringing to birth until
Christ is formed in you! My young people have gone along a harsh path. Now Susanna has been ensnared
by the two lawless elders. Now they strip the young and beautiful woman naked, so that they may satisfy themselves with her beauty.
And now they bring false accusations against her. There is a famine, not of bread, nor a thirst for water,
but for hearing the word of the Lord. Now all the virgins have grown drowsy and fallen asleep.
For the saying of the Lord Jesus has been fulfilled: “Will the Son of Man find faith on earth?”
I hear that each person is betraying his neighbor, so that what was spoken may be fulfilled:
“Brother will betray brother to death.” Or, “Satan has asked to have you,
to sift you like wheat.” But let no one think, children, that the Lord has grown weak.
Rather, we have. For he says, “Or can my hand not rescue you? Or has my hearing grown dull, so that I cannot hear?”
But your sins stand between us and God. For we have grown lazy, and others, treating things with contempt,
have committed lawlessness. By plundering one another and devouring one another, we have brought death upon ourselves.
Yet our righteousness ought to have far exceeded that of the scribes and Pharisees.
For I hear that the Jews are inviting some of you to their assemblies. Therefore take care that no sin,
whether great or small, or deliberate, touches you. Let not one of you commit
the great sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Do not join them, the rulers of Sodom
and the people of Gomorrah, whose hands are full of blood. But we have neither killed a prophet,
nor betrayed Christ, nor crucified him. Why should I say much to you? Remember what you have heard,
and now speak of what you were taught, since you have also heard this:
that the Jews said, “Christ was a man, and he died a violent death.”
Then let them tell us: after whose violent death was the whole world filled with disciples?
For what man who died a violent death did so many disciples and others with them
die for the name of their teacher? In the name of what man who died a violent death
have demons been driven out for so many years? And how many great deeds [?] take place in the universal Church!
Yet they do not understand that one who takes himself out of life of his own will dies under compulsion.
After he had said this, he ordered them to hurry and come out of the prison.
The temple warden and the governor Theophilus came to them with a large crowd, saying:
“Look, your elder Euctemon has surrendered and offered sacrifice. You too should come to an agreement, for Lepidon is questioning you.”
and Euctemon. Pionius said, “Those who have been put in prison—
it is right for them to await the proconsul, so that we may see what he orders concerning them.” After saying much to them, they went away.
They came again with a large crowd. The prefect Theophilus said, “The proconsul [?] has sent orders for you to be taken to Ephesus.”
Pionius said, “Let the man who was sent come and take us.” Theophilus said, “But the chief officer is more distinguished,
and you should go to him instead. If you refuse, I am a magistrate, and I will do what I wish.”
He bound him by the neck and handed him over to the soldiers to lead away, so that they nearly strangled him. Then he came into the streets, and Sabina too,
the two of them crying out loudly, “We are Christians!” and throwing themselves to the ground
so that they would not be taken into the idol temple. Six soldiers carried Pionius head downward.
Unable to hold him, they struck his ribs with their knees and dragged him by his hands and feet as he cried out.
Those carrying him brought him in and laid him on the ground in the idol temple. Meanwhile, Euctemon was standing
beside the idol temple. Lepidus said, “Why do you not offer sacrifice, Pionius?”
Pionius said, “Because we are Christians.” Lepidus said, “What god do you worship?”
Pionius said, “The one who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them.”
Lepidus said, “Who, then, is the crucified one?” Pionius said, “The one whom God sent for the salvation of the world.”
The magistrates shouted loudly and laughed, and Lepidus began to curse him.
But Pionius cried out, “God is faithful. Do not be ashamed; honor justice.
Recognize those who are your equals. Follow your own laws.
Punish us as disobedient people; you yourselves are disobedient. You have been ordered to punish us, not to compel us.”
A certain Rufinus stood before him, a man skilled in rhetoric.
He said, “Stop, Pionius; do not boast.” But he replied to him, “Is this your rhetoric? Is this what your books teach?
Did Socrates not suffer these things at the hands of the Athenians? Did Socrates, Aristides, Anaxarchus,
and the others boast—those who loved philosophy, justice, and endurance?”
A certain man of high rank and worldly honor said, “Do not shout, Pionius.”
Pionius said, “Do not compel us. Instead, light the pyre, and we will climb onto it ourselves.”
A certain Terentius shouted from the crowd, “You know that this man is also encouraging others not to offer sacrifice!”
And so they put wreaths on the two of them, but they tore them apart and threw them away.
The public slave stood holding food sacrificed to an idol, but he did not dare approach anyone.
Instead, the public slave himself ate some of it in front of everyone, while the two cried out, “We are Christians!”
Not knowing what to do, they led them back to prison. The crowd mocked them and slapped
him. Someone said to Sabina, “Could you not have died in your own homeland?” She said, “What is my homeland?”
“I am Pionius’s sister.” Asclepiades said to Pionius, “Are you not afraid of me over this?”
And so the two were led into prison. As Pionius was entering the prison,
one of the soldiers struck him on the head so hard that he injured him. But he remained silent.
The hands and sides of the man who had struck him became inflamed, so that he could barely breathe.
When the two had entered the prison, they praised God because they had remained unharmed in Christ’s name,
and the enemy had not triumphed over them. They continued in songs and prayers, strengthening themselves.
Afterward, the proconsul came to Smyrna. Pionius was brought before him, and when the proconsul had taken his seat on the judgment seat,
he began questioning him: “What is your name?” He answered, “My name is Pionius.” The proconsul said,
“Will you sacrifice?” He answered, “No.” The proconsul asked, “What faith do you hold?”
He answered, “I am a priest of the catholic Church.” The proconsul said, “Are you their teacher?”
He answered, “Yes.” The proconsul said, “You are a teacher of foolishness.”
Pionius answered, “I belong to God’s faith, and I believe in the Lord who created all things.”
The proconsul said, “Sacrifice.” He answered, “No. I have learned to believe in God in a manner worthy of him.” The proconsul said,
“We all honor the gods, both heaven and the gods who are in heaven. Why are you looking up at the air? Look at it.”
He answered, “I am not looking up at the air, but toward the one who created the air, heaven, and everything in heaven.”
The proconsul said, “Say who created them.” He answered, “It is not fitting to say.”
The proconsul said, “Then the god is Zeus, who is in heaven,
for he is king of all the gods.” Pionius remained silent. When he had been hung up, they said, “Sacrifice.”
He answered, “No.” After torturing him again with claws, they said, “Repent.” He answered, “I have not lost my senses,
but I fear the living God.” The proconsul said, “Many others have sacrificed too, and they are alive and in their right minds.”
He answered, “I do not sacrifice.” The proconsul said, “Why are you eager for death?”
Pionius said, “I am not eager for death, but for life.” The proconsul said, “You are doing nothing remarkable by being eager for death.
But since you are indeed eager for death, let yourself be burned alive.”
And they wrote on tablets in Latin: “Pionius, who has confessed himself to be a Christian,
we have ordered to be burned alive.” When he went eagerly to the place of judgment,
and the prison officer arrived, he stripped himself. Then the pure man, seeing the beauty of his own body,
was filled with great joy. Looking up to heaven, he gave praise to God, who had thus
preserved him. He stretched himself out on the wooden stake and gave himself over to the soldier to be nailed to it. When he had been nailed down,
the public executioner again said, “Change your mind, and we will remove the nails.”
But he answered, “I have felt that they are nothing. Therefore I am eager to rise at once,”
demonstrating the resurrection from the dead. So they set him upright on the stake.
Then afterward they also set up a certain priest named Metrodorus, of the Marcionite faith. It happened that Pionius was placed on the right,
and Metrodorus on the left. Both faced east. When the wood had been brought
and laid around them, Pionius closed his eyes, so that the crowd thought he had breathed his last.
But he was praying in secret. When he reached the end of his prayer, he opened his eyes.
While the flames were still high, his face was joyful. Finally, after saying “Amen” and saying to the Lord, “Receive my soul,”
he breathed his last quietly and without pain, as though letting out a breath, and surrendered his spirit to the Lord.
All his blood, all his soul, having been unjustly condemned, and having promised to preserve [?].
Thus the blessed Pionius lived his life, blameless and undefiled, always keeping his mind directed toward God Almighty
and toward the mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ our God. Of such an
end he was found worthy. Having won the great struggle, he passed through the narrow gates
into the broad and great light. His crown was revealed through his body, for when we came after the fire, we saw him like this:
the martyr’s body was like a young man’s, made smooth, and his ears were bright.
His beard shone like that of someone whose beard was only just beginning to grow. His face was bright again, and his grace was wondrous,
so that the Christians were strengthened still more in their faith.
But the unbelievers became afraid and, having [?], went away in fear.
Saint Pionius suffered martyrdom on March 12, a Saturday, at the tenth hour, under Emperor [?].
But our Lord Jesus Christ reigns over us. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
